hints: Look at the sloping line from P at velocity $u$ to S at velocity $v$ and recall that distance is the area under this velocity-time line from $0$ to $t$.
Split the required trapezium NPSU into a lower rectangle of height $u$ plus an upper triangle of height $v-u$, or use average velocity $(u+v)/2$ times $t$.
Check each listed sum at time $t/2$ with vertical line RVW: test whether the left part plus the right part rebuilds exactly the area below PS down to the time axis.
walkthrough: Identify the distance as the area under the velocity-time graph between time $0$ and time $t$, which is the trapezium NPSU bounded by line PS, the velocity axis and the line $t$.
For uniform acceleration the area is average velocity times time: $s = \frac{u+v}{2} \times t$.
Examine the division at $t/2$: NPWV is the left rectangle $u \times t/2$ and VRSU is the right rectangle $v \times t/2$ up to the dashed line QS.
Add them: $u t/2 + v t/2 = (u+v)t/2$, which matches the area under PS and therefore the distance travelled.

options.A: NPTU is $u \times t$ and PQST is $(v-u) \times t$, so their sum is $vt$ which is larger than the trapezium under line PS.
options.B: NPWV is $u \times t/2$ and VRSU is $v \times t/2$, so their sum is $(u+v)t/2$ which equals the area under PS from $0$ to $t$.
options.C: WRST is only the upper small rectangle $(v-u) \times t/2$, so adding NPWV gives $ut/2 + (v-u)t/2$ which is less than the full area under PS.
options.D: PST + PQS equals the triangular increase $(v-u)t/2 + (v-u)t/2$, which omits the rectangle $u \times t$ due to the initial velocity $u$.
